title: Choosing the vehicle: what an entity is for, and the three documents that make it real
summary: An entity is a legal container that holds an asset, takes on its risks and speaks with its own signature. This lesson explains the main vehicle types, the five questions that choose between them, why serious developers put each project in its own special purpose vehicle, and why a minute book, resolutions and a signing authority are what make the container actually work.
body:
Mr Shabazz, an entity is a container you build around a project so that its risks, its money and its decisions stay inside. Choose the container for the job it must do, then keep its records as if a judge will read them, because one day a lender, an auditor or a court will.

Recall

Q. What makes a land contract bind before closing?

A. What the document says and how the parties behave, not its title. A signed letter of intent with complete essential terms and no non-binding statement can come close to a contract.

Q. What is an option premium, and what happens to it if you exercise?

A. The fee paid for the exclusive right to buy later at an agreed price. Whether it is credited against the price on exercise is a negotiated term; it usually should be.

Q. How do rising interest rates tend to affect cap rates and land values?

A. Higher rates usually push cap rates up over time, which lowers completed values and therefore residual land values. The link is a tendency, not a fixed rule.

Why this matters

Every number you have learned so far assumes someone owns the project. Who that someone is decides who is liable if it fails, how the profit is taxed, whether a lender will fund it, who can make decisions, what passes on your death, and how you can sell. Those are Omar's six lenses, and the entity is where all six meet. Pick it casually at the start and you will spend money and time fixing it later, sometimes at a tax cost you cannot undo.

The main vehicles, in plain English

  • Corporation. A separate legal person owned by shareholders and run by directors. Its debts are generally its own, so shareholders risk what they invested. It is usually taxed on its own profits.
  • General partnership. Two or more people carrying on business together. Usually each partner is personally liable for the partnership's obligations, including those created by the other partners. Rarely right for development.
  • Limited partnership. A general partner, often a corporation, that manages and carries unlimited liability, and limited partners who invest and whose liability is generally limited if they do not take part in management. Common for investor-funded projects because it can be treated as flow-through for tax in some systems.
  • Limited liability company. A United States form combining limited liability with flexible tax treatment. Its treatment outside the United States can differ; verify against the primary source.
  • Contractual joint venture. Two parties cooperate by contract without a new entity. Simple to start, but liability and ownership can be unclear.
  • Trust. A relationship in which a trustee holds property for beneficiaries. Used in estate and some investment structures; Tessa covers it later in the course.

The professional framing: no vehicle is best in general. Each is a different bundle of liability, tax, financing, governance and exit characteristics, and the right choice depends on who the owners are and where they are resident. Professional sign-off required: a corporate lawyer and a tax adviser, together, before you form anything.

The five questions that choose the vehicle

  1. Liability. If this project fails or is sued, what must the container protect?
  2. Tax. Should profit be taxed inside the entity or flow through to the owners, and where are they resident?
  3. Financing. What will the lender insist on? Construction lenders commonly want a single-purpose entity that owns only the project.
  4. Governance. Who decides what, and how are disputes broken?
  5. Exit and estate. Will you sell the building or the entity, and what happens to your interest if you die or become incapable?

Say that out loud now.

Liability, tax, financing, governance, exit. The vehicle that answers all five for these owners is the right one.

Worked example one: one company or three?

Hypothetical. You hold three projects in one corporation: a finished 20-unit building with 2 million dollars of equity in it, a project under construction, and a site in approvals. The project under construction suffers a contractor insolvency and a 3 million dollar cost overrun its lender will not fund. Creditors of that project can pursue the corporation, and the corporation owns the finished building. Your stable asset is now exposed to your riskiest one.

Now hold each project in its own special purpose vehicle, owned by a holding company. The overrun stays inside the construction SPV. The finished building's SPV is a separate legal person with its own creditors. This is called ring-fencing. It is not absolute: a personal guarantee you sign, or a court disregarding the structure for misuse, can reach across it, as LEX taught in Week 21. But it changes the default answer from "everything is exposed" to "this project is exposed."

Worked example two: the landowner venture

From Week 33: a landowner contributing land worth 2.25 million dollars and you contributing 5.3 million of cash. A common shape is a limited partnership that owns the project, with a general partner corporation you control that manages it, and both of you as limited partners. The limited partnership agreement carries the waterfall from Week 33. The general partner corporation signs contracts, and its minute book records each decision. Whether this is the right shape depends on tax residence and local law; verify against the primary source.

The three documents that make it real

An entity exists on paper, and it only protects you if the paper is kept. A minute book is the official record of the entity: its constating documents, registers of directors, officers and shareholders, and the minutes and resolutions of every formal decision. A resolution is the formal record that the directors or the owners approved something, such as buying land or borrowing money. A signing authority defines who may sign what on the entity's behalf, and up to what amount. Day 4 covers the law; today the principle is that the entity acts only through these documents, so a decision with no resolution or a signature with no authority is a gap someone else will exploit.

How the best do it

Large institutional property owners generally hold each significant asset in its own special purpose vehicle under holding companies, keep an entity register listing every vehicle with its directors, owners and bank accounts, and run a corporate secretarial function that keeps every minute book current. A small developer can copy the core cheaply: one SPV per project, a one-page entity chart, and an annual calendar of filings and minutes kept by a named person.

The biggest risk

Forming the entity after you have already signed in your own name. Contracts, deposits and invoices in your personal name may stay yours, with the liability attached. The control: form the project entity before signing anything binding about the project, or sign expressly for an entity to be formed, with your lawyer's drafting. Day 2 shows the cost of getting this wrong.

The beginner's mistake

Copying a friend's structure. A structure that suited one person's residence, family and financing can be wrong, and expensive, for yours.

Six-Lens Check

Tax: the vehicle decides where profit is taxed and in whose hands; verify against the primary source. Liability: the vehicle sets the default ring-fence, which guarantees can override. Banking: lenders want single-purpose borrowers with clean records and clear signing authority. Governance: decision rights live in the articles, the agreements and the minutes. Estate: shares or units in a vehicle pass under your estate plan, so the plan must name them. Exit: selling an SPV's shares and selling its building are different transactions with different consequences.

Callback

In Week 21, LEX and I taught limited liability and the ways a court can pierce the corporate veil. This lesson is the practical side of that warning: the minute book, the resolutions and the signing authority are the evidence that the entity was run as a real, separate person.

Recap

Choose the vehicle by liability, tax, financing, governance and exit, for these owners. Put each project in its own SPV under a holding company. Make the entity real through its minute book, resolutions and signing authority. Next: Ford, with Cole, on money spent before the company existed.
checklist: Answer the five questions before choosing any vehicle
Form the project entity before signing anything binding about the project
Hold each project in its own special purpose vehicle
Keep a one-page entity chart of every vehicle and its owners
Keep each minute book current with every formal decision
Record a signing authority with limits for every entity
Have a corporate lawyer and a tax adviser approve the structure together
Name each entity interest in your estate plan
head: Field checklist
speak: An entity is a legal container around a project. A corporation is a separate person owned by shareholders and run by directors. A general partnership usually exposes every partner. A limited partnership has a managing general partner and investors with limited liability. A limited liability company is a United States form. Choose by five questions: liability, tax, financing, governance, and exit and estate. Serious developers put each project in its own special purpose vehicle under a holding company, so a disaster on one project does not reach the others. That ring-fence is not absolute; guarantees and misuse can cross it. The entity only works through three documents: a current minute book, resolutions recording each formal decision, and a signing authority saying who may sign what. Form the entity before you sign anything binding, and get legal and tax advice together.
terms: Special purpose vehicle — an entity formed to own and carry out a single project, separating its assets and liabilities from others.
Minute book — the official record of an entity's constating documents, registers, minutes and resolutions.
Signing authority — the defined power of named people to sign documents and commit an entity, often with limits by amount or type.

hostile.q: As your construction lender, I need to know: who exactly is the borrower, and who can bind it?
hostile.a: The borrower is the project's special purpose vehicle, which owns only this site. Here is its certificate, the register of directors and shareholders, the resolution approving this loan, and the signing authority naming who may sign loan documents and up to what amount. Our holding company owns the shares, and the entity chart shows the whole structure on one page.

role: Failure forensics (with Cole, audit and integrity)
title: Money spent before the company existed: a composite
summary: A developer spent heavily on a site in his own name before the project company was formed, then could not prove which costs belonged to the project. Partners disputed them, the lender would not count them as equity, and the tax treatment was unclear. This composite case runs the seven steps and ends with the rule that keeps pre-incorporation spending clean.
body:
Mr Shabazz, money spent on a project before its company exists is the easiest money to lose, because nobody can prove later whose it was, what it bought or what it should count for. This case shows how a quarter of a million dollars of real work became an argument.

Recall

Q. When you reverse engineer an asking price, what question are you answering?

A. What must be true about value, cost, approvals and timing for that price to be rational. If the required assumptions are not credible, the price is not either.

Q. In the composite handshake case, why did the developer's leverage disappear?

A. Because once the approval succeeded, the landowner held a valuable asset and had a cash buyer, and the developer had no signed agreement recording his interest.

Q. What is the danger of buying land late in a property cycle?

A. Prices reflect peak values and easy credit, and a downturn during approvals or construction can cut completed values and remove financing just as the project needs it.

Why this matters

Every project begins before its company does. You pay for a survey, a feasibility study, an option premium, a planner, a lawyer. Those early costs are real equity in the project if they are recorded properly, and a liability or a dispute if they are not. A small developer spends more of his own money in this early period than at any other time, so this is where clean records pay most. This is a composite example built from recurring patterns; names and numbers are invented.

The case in seven steps

Step 1, timeline. Months 1 to 9: a developer pursues a site. He pays a 60,000 dollar option premium, design fees, studies and legal fees, about 250,000 dollars in total, from his personal account and a personal credit card. Some invoices are addressed to him, some to a company he owns for another business, and some to a project name that is not yet a legal entity. Month 10: he forms a project company and brings in two equity partners. Month 12: the construction lender asks for evidence of equity contributed. Month 13: one partner asks why the developer's capital account shows 250,000 dollars of contribution when only 140,000 is supported by invoices clearly for this project. Month 15: the partners dispute the figure, the lender counts only the supported costs as equity, and the developer's accountant cannot say with confidence how the costs will be treated for tax.

Step 2, key decisions. Spending without a project entity or a written agreement for an entity to be formed. Mixing payment sources and invoice names. Signing the option in his personal name with no right to assign it. Admitting partners without a documented, agreed schedule of pre-formation costs.

Step 3, assumptions. That everyone would accept his word on what he had spent. That costs could be "moved into the company later" without consequence. That the option, signed personally, would simply belong to the company once it existed. That the lender would count everything he had spent.

Step 4, incentives. The developer wanted the largest possible capital credit for early costs, because it increased his share. The new partners wanted the smallest, because it diluted theirs. The lender wanted to count only equity it could verify. Each incentive was legitimate; with no agreed record, they could only collide.

Step 5, warning signs ignored. His accountant had asked twice for a project cost log. A partner's lawyer had requested a schedule of pre-formation costs before signing. The option agreement had a clause restricting assignment. All three were treated as paperwork rather than as risk.

Step 6, point of no return. Admitting the partners without a signed, agreed schedule of pre-formation costs and an assignment of the option to the company. After that, every unsupported dollar became a negotiation the developer was likely to lose.

Step 7, root cause. No boundary between the developer's personal money and the project's money before the project company existed. Without a boundary, nothing could prove which side of it a cost fell on.

Say that out loud now.

Draw the boundary before the first dollar: whose money, which project, what it bought.

Worked example one: what the missing records cost

Hypothetical round numbers. Of 250,000 dollars spent, 140,000 is supported by invoices clearly addressed to and describing this project. Another 70,000 is plausibly for the project but invoiced to his other company. The final 40,000 is credit card spending with no invoices. The partners agree to credit 140,000 in full and half of the 70,000, which is 35,000, and nothing for the 40,000. His capital credit is 175,000 dollars instead of 250,000. If the project's equity totals 2.5 million dollars, 75,000 dollars of lost credit is 3 percentage points of ownership, which on a project that later makes 1.5 million dollars of profit is worth roughly 45,000 dollars, before any preferred return. The work was real; the proof was not.

Worked example two: the option he could not transfer

The option was signed in his personal name and restricted assignment without the owner's consent. To put the site into the company, he needed the owner's written consent. By month 10 the land had risen in value and the owner asked for 75,000 dollars to consent. One missing clause, a right to assign to an affiliate, cost more than the option premium itself. Professional sign-off required: a real estate lawyer, on assignment rights, before you sign any option.

Cole's audit note

Cole would look for four records. A project cost log started on day one, listing each cost with date, payee, description and payment source. Invoices addressed to the project entity or to "an entity to be formed." A written pre-formation agreement stating how early costs will be credited when the company exists. And a signed assignment of every early contract, including the option, to the company. Cole would also check whether any expenditure was disguised personal spending, because an auditor who finds one such item stops trusting the rest of the log.

Reading it from the partners' side

The partners were not being greedy. Every dollar of unproven credit they accepted came straight out of their own ownership, and they owed it to their own investors to accept only what they could defend. A partner who credits an unsupported cost because the developer seems honest is taking a risk that partner's lawyer will rightly refuse. Seen that way, the dispute was not about trust at all. It was about evidence, and the developer was the only person in the room who could have produced it, months earlier, at almost no cost. The lesson for you is to arrive at the partner meeting with the schedule already prepared, so the conversation is about terms rather than proof.

The biggest risk

Treating early spending as informal because the amounts feel small. In a small project, early costs can be a large share of a developer's own equity. The control is a project cost log, one payment source and a pre-formation agreement from the first dollar.

The beginner's mistake

Believing that a cost can be moved into the company later without consequence. Moving it may require partner agreement, lender acceptance and a tax treatment that depends on how it is done; verify against the primary source.

Callback

In Week 12, Nadia taught capitalised costs and work in progress: costs that build an asset are recorded on the balance sheet, not expensed. That only works if the costs are recorded to the right entity with evidence. Pre-formation spending is the first test of Nadia's discipline, and the one most often failed.

Recap

A developer spent 250,000 dollars before forming the project company, through mixed accounts, mixed invoice names and a personal option he could not assign. Partners, the lender and the tax adviser each discounted what he could not prove. Rule 35 below is the control. Next: Nadia on The Money, what the entity costs and what it saves.
checklist: Start a project cost log on the first day of pursuing a site
Pay project costs from one dedicated account
Address invoices to the project entity or an entity to be formed
Sign a pre-formation agreement on how early costs will be credited
Include a right to assign to an affiliate in every early contract
Assign every early contract to the company when it is formed
Agree a schedule of pre-formation costs before admitting partners
head: Field checklist
rule: Rule 35: From the first dollar, every project cost is logged, paid from one source, invoiced to the project or an entity to be formed, and assignable to it; nothing is moved into the company later on my word alone.
speak: This is a composite case. A developer spent about 250,000 dollars pursuing a site before forming the project company: an option premium, design, studies and legal fees, paid from personal accounts and a credit card, with invoices in three different names. When he brought in partners, only 140,000 dollars was clearly provable. The partners credited 175,000, the lender counted only what it could verify, and his accountant could not be sure of the tax treatment. The option, signed personally with no right to assign, cost him 75,000 dollars in consent fees to move into the company. The root cause was no boundary between his money and the project's money before the company existed. Rule 35: from the first dollar, every cost is logged, paid from one source, invoiced to the project and assignable to it.
terms: Pre-formation costs — costs incurred on a project before the entity that will own it is legally formed.
Project cost log — a running record of each project cost with date, payee, description, amount and payment source.
Assignment clause — a contract term stating whether and how a party may transfer its rights to another, such as an affiliate.

hostile.q: You say you put 250,000 dollars into this project before we joined. We can see 140,000 dollars of evidence. Why should we credit the rest?
hostile.a: You should credit what I can prove. Here is the cost log with every invoice. The 140,000 is clearly for this project. For the 70,000 invoiced to my other company, here is the work product each invoice bought, and I propose we credit what that evidence supports. The 40,000 without invoices I withdraw. From today, every cost runs through the company's account.

title: What an entity costs and what it saves: running costs, ring-fencing and tax leakage
summary: Every entity has a running cost, and every structure moves where and when tax is paid. This lesson prices the annual cost of special purpose vehicles against the exposure they protect, shows how the same profit reaches an owner in different amounts through different structures, and closes with Warrick on money that sits inside a company.
body:
Mr Shabazz, an entity is not free: it costs money every year to keep, and it changes how much of the profit reaches you and when. Price both before you choose, because the cheapest structure to set up is often the most expensive to live with.

Recall

Q. In the mock go or no-go meeting, what decides the outcome?

A. Whether the written evidence on demand, approvals, cost and land price supports the decision at the downside case, not how strongly anyone in the room feels.

Q. Why will a lender not fund an option premium?

A. Because an option gives it no useful security: if you default, there is no land to sell. The premium and extensions come from equity.

Q. What does a higher interest rate do to a development's residual land value?

A. It raises finance costs and usually pushes cap rates up, which lowers completed value. Both reduce what is left for land.

Why this matters

Owners often choose a structure on one feature, such as limited liability or a tax rate they heard about, and discover the running costs and the cost of getting money out only later. A structure is a machine you operate for years. Each year it needs filings, books, bank accounts and sometimes a review or audit. And every dollar of profit travels through it before it reaches you, losing some to tax along the way. You need to see both costs in numbers, side by side, before the structure is formed, because unwinding an entity later can itself trigger tax and fees.

The running cost of an entity

Plain English first. Each entity needs its own legal filings, its own bookkeeping, its own bank account, its own tax return, and often its own insurance and its own year-end accounts. The professional term for the tax lost as money moves through a structure is leakage; the running cost is simply overhead, but it is overhead you must model.

Worked example one, hypothetical round numbers. Suppose each special purpose vehicle costs about 8,000 dollars a year in filings, bookkeeping, accounts and bank fees. Three projects in three SPVs under a holding company cost about 32,000 dollars a year including the holding company; three projects in one company cost about 10,000 dollars.

Now price what the extra 22,000 dollars a year buys. You have 2 million dollars of equity in a finished building. Suppose you judge a 5 percent chance in a given year that a construction project suffers a loss its own assets cannot cover and creditors look to the wider company. If that happens in the single-company structure, the finished building's 2 million of equity is exposed; say you would lose half of it. Expected exposure: 0.05 times 1 million, which is 50,000 dollars a year. On these numbers, spending 22,000 a year to protect against 50,000 of expected exposure is good value. With one small project and no stable asset, the answer may reverse. The probability is a judgement, written down with reasons; the costs are illustrative, not quotes.

Tax leakage: the same profit, three paths

The second cost is where and when tax falls. The rates below are invented for teaching and are not any jurisdiction's actual rates. Verify every real rate against the primary source, and take advice from a licensed tax adviser.

Worked example two. A project makes 1,000,000 dollars of taxable profit.

  1. Path A, taxed inside a corporation, then paid out as a dividend. Corporate tax at a hypothetical 25 percent leaves 750,000 dollars. A tax on the dividend in your hands at a hypothetical 15 percent costs 112,500, leaving 637,500 dollars. Total leakage: 362,500.
  2. Path B, flow-through, taxed only in your hands. A partnership whose profit is taxed directly to you at a hypothetical 40 percent leaves 600,000 dollars. Total leakage: 400,000.
  3. Path C, taxed inside the corporation and retained for the next project. Corporate tax leaves 750,000 dollars working in the business. No second layer yet. The dividend tax is deferred, not avoided, until you take the money out.

Three lessons, none of them a recommendation. First, the order of the paths changes when the rates change, so never decide on one rate you heard about. Second, timing matters as much as rate: Path C keeps more money working today, which may be worth more than a lower final tax. Third, many systems try to make the two layers of tax roughly equal to one layer, an idea called integration, so the gap is often smaller than people expect; verify how it works where you are.

Say that out loud now.

Price the running cost, price the leakage, and price the timing. Then choose.

What the lender counts

A lender counts equity it can verify in the borrowing entity. Cash paid by the SPV from its own account, with invoices in its name, is easy to count. Costs paid personally before the SPV existed, as in Day 2, may be counted only if documented and formally contributed. So the structure is also a financing tool: a clean SPV with clean books makes your equity visible, and visible equity is what the loan is sized against.

Warrick's Wealth Ledger

On your personal balance sheet, money inside a company is not your cash. Your asset is the shares, and getting the money out has a tax cost and sometimes needs partner or lender consent. Warrick asks you to record two figures for every entity you own: its value, and its after-extraction value, which is what would reach you after the tax and costs of taking it out. Your liquidity floor must be met from money that is already personal and accessible, never from cash trapped in a project company. A licensed adviser is required before you act.

Working with advisers

Structure is where you depend most on advisers and where they most often work in silos. A corporate lawyer forms the entity, an accountant files its returns, a tax adviser designs the leakage, and none of them sees the whole. Ask them to review the structure together, at least once, and give each the entity chart, the financing terms and your residence facts. Write down the question you are asking each one, and ask each to state what they did not look at.

When two advisers disagree, do not pick the one you prefer. Put the disagreement in writing, ask each to respond to the other's reasoning, and decide on the evidence. If you cannot follow the reasoning, that is a sign to ask again, not to nod. Their fees are a cost of the structure; your judgement about their advice is your job.

The biggest risk

Choosing a structure on its tax result alone and discovering that the lender will not lend to it, the partners cannot invest through it, or it cannot be sold without a large tax charge. The control: test every proposed structure against all five questions from Day 1 before forming it.

The beginner's mistake

Forgetting the running cost of entities that no longer do anything. A dormant SPV still files, still needs a minute book kept and can still be fined for missed filings. Wind up what you no longer need, on advice.

Callback

In Week 11 you learned that cash and profit are different. Here they diverge again: a structure can report the same profit while delivering very different cash to you at different times. Always ask how much reaches you, and when.

Recap

Price each entity's running cost against the exposure it ring-fences. Price leakage and timing on the actual rates, verified. Keep the SPV's books clean so your equity is visible to the lender. Record the after-extraction value of every entity on your balance sheet, and get your advisers to review the structure together. Next: LEX on The Rules, minute books, resolutions and signing authority, with a Canada and Guyana comparison.
checklist: Estimate the annual running cost of every entity you form
Compare the cost of extra SPVs with the exposure they protect
Model leakage on verified actual rates, never on remembered ones
Model the timing of tax as well as its amount
Pay project costs from the SPV's own account so equity is visible
Record the value and after-extraction value of each entity you own
Have your lawyer, accountant and tax adviser review the structure together
Wind up dormant entities on advice
head: Field checklist
speak: An entity costs money every year, and it changes how much profit reaches you and when. If each SPV costs about 8,000 dollars a year, three SPVs under a holding company cost about 22,000 dollars a year more than one company. That is good value if it ring-fences, say, 50,000 dollars a year of expected exposure to a stable building. Then price leakage. With invented rates, profit taxed in a corporation and paid as a dividend, profit flowing through to you, and profit retained in the company each deliver different amounts at different times. The order changes with the rates, and timing can matter as much as rate. Lenders count equity they can verify in the SPV. On your balance sheet, money in a company is not your cash; record its after-extraction value, and get your advisers to review the structure together.
terms: Leakage — the tax and cost lost as money moves through a structure before it reaches the owner.
Integration — a tax design idea that aims to make profit taxed through a company and then to the owner bear roughly the same total tax as profit earned directly.
After-extraction value — what would reach the owner personally after the tax and costs of taking money out of an entity.

hostile.q: Your structure has four entities for three projects. Isn't that just paying accountants to feel safe?
hostile.a: It costs about 22,000 dollars a year more than one company. In exchange, a loss on the project under construction cannot reach the 2 million dollars of equity in our finished building, which I estimate as about 50,000 dollars a year of expected exposure. If we had one small project and no stable asset, I would use fewer entities. The choice is priced, not assumed.

title: How a company speaks: directors, resolutions, minute books and signing authority
summary: A company is a separate legal person that can only act through people, and the law decides which people and on what record. This lesson covers who holds which powers, what a resolution is and when one is needed, what belongs in a minute book, how signing authority and apparent authority work, the trap of contracts signed before incorporation, and a Canada and Guyana comparison.
body:
Mr Shabazz, a company has no hands. It acts only through directors, officers and agents, and only on decisions it can prove it made. The minute book and the signing authority are that proof, and a lender, a buyer or a court will ask for them.

Recall

Q. In the checkpoint mock interview, what did the hard question always test?

A. Whether you could say what you would do when the evidence went against the deal, which is reprice, hold back or walk, calmly and without defending a position.

Q. What separates an option from a right of first refusal?

A. An option lets you buy when you choose at a fixed price; a right of first refusal only lets you match an offer the owner is willing to accept from someone else.

Q. Name one way government action can move a property cycle.

A. Changes to interest-rate policy, lending rules, zoning or approval speed can each change how much new supply is built and when, which shifts the cycle.

Why this matters

You will sign loan documents, land contracts and construction contracts on behalf of companies you control. If the company never formally decided to sign, or the person signing had no authority, the document may not bind the company, or may bind you personally instead. Lenders know this, so they demand certified resolutions and proof of authority before they fund. Getting this right is cheap and routine. Getting it wrong can delay a closing, void a deal or put liability where you did not intend.

The separate person and its three groups

Plain English first. Once formed, a corporation is a legal person separate from its owners; the classic English case Salomon v A Salomon and Co Ltd, decided in 1897, is still taught for that principle. But it acts only through people, in three groups.

  • Shareholders own the company. They usually elect directors and approve fundamental changes, such as amending the constating documents, selling substantially all the assets or winding up.
  • Directors manage or supervise the business. They generally owe duties to the company, commonly described as a duty of loyalty, acting honestly and in its best interests, and a duty of care. The precise content varies; verify against the primary source.
  • Officers, such as a president or secretary, are appointed by the directors to run day-to-day affairs within the authority given to them.

In a small company you may be all three. The law still treats them as different hats, and the records should show which hat you were wearing.

Resolutions and the minute book

A resolution is a formal decision of the directors or the shareholders. It can be passed at a meeting with a quorum, meaning the minimum number present, or in many systems by a written resolution signed by all those entitled to vote. Some decisions need an ordinary majority of shareholders and some a higher, special majority; which decisions and what thresholds depend on the statute and the company's own articles, so verify against the primary source.

The minute book is where these live. A complete one usually holds the constating documents and any by-laws, registers of directors, officers and shareholders, a share or unit ledger, minutes and resolutions in date order, any unanimous shareholder agreement, and, where the law requires it, a register of individuals with significant control. If a director has a personal interest in a contract, most systems require it to be disclosed and recorded, and the director may need to abstain.

Worked example one, hypothetical. Your SPV is borrowing 15 million dollars. The lender's counsel asks for a certified copy of the directors' resolution approving the loan and authorising named officers to sign, a certificate of incumbency confirming who holds office, the constating documents, and evidence of good standing. If you hold the only director's seat, a written resolution signed by you, dated before the loan documents, does the job. If the resolution is dated after you signed, or names the wrong entity, the closing stalls while it is fixed. Professional sign-off required: a corporate lawyer, for every closing resolution.

Say that out loud now.

Decide first, record it, then sign. In that order, every time.

Signing authority, actual and apparent

Actual authority is the power the company actually gave a person, by resolution, by-law or appointment. Apparent authority, in concept, is the authority an outsider can reasonably believe a person has because of how the company presented them. A company can sometimes be bound by someone acting within apparent authority even if it never gave actual authority. Related to this, many common-law systems have an "indoor management" rule, traced to Royal British Bank v Turquand in 1856, under which an outsider dealing in good faith need not check that internal procedures were followed. Statutes have since modified these rules, so verify how they apply.

The practical answer is a written signing authority matrix: who may sign what, up to which amount, alone or with a second signatory. Worked example two, hypothetical. Your matrix says any officer may sign contracts up to 50,000 dollars, two signatures are needed up to 500,000 dollars, and anything above needs a directors' resolution. Your site manager signs a 300,000 dollar change order alone. Whether the company is bound may turn on apparent authority, but internally the matrix has been breached, the cost control has failed, and your lender's monitor will ask why. Give the contractor a copy of the matrix at contract signing, so he knows who can bind you.

Contracts signed before the company exists

Day 2 showed the commercial cost. The legal concept: in many systems, a person who signs a contract for a company not yet formed can be personally bound unless the company, once formed, adopts the contract, and sometimes even then. The safest path is to form the company first. If you cannot, sign expressly "for an entity to be formed," with a clause releasing you once the company adopts the contract, drafted by your lawyer. Verify the statutory rule where you operate.

Two Systems: Canada and Guyana

A conceptual comparison only; verify against the primary source. Canada: you can incorporate federally or in a province, and each statute sets its own rules on directors, resolutions, records and residency requirements for directors where they exist. Federally incorporated private companies have been required in recent years to keep a register of individuals with significant control, and some provinces have similar rules [unverified — confirm independently]. Guyana: companies are governed by a companies statute and registered with a public registry, and the country has introduced beneficial ownership disclosure requirements for companies [unverified — confirm independently]. The common thread is direction of travel: both systems increasingly expect a company to be able to show who really owns and controls it, so keep that record current.

The biggest risk

Backdating or fabricating a resolution to cover a decision that was never made. It can be treated as a misrepresentation to a lender and may be an offence. The control: if a resolution is missing, pass a new one now that ratifies the earlier act, dated truthfully, on your lawyer's advice.

The beginner's mistake

Letting the minute book lapse because "it is only my company." Gaps are found at the worst time: a refinancing, a sale or a dispute with a partner.

Callback

In Week 25, LEX and Vera taught that an engagement letter must say who the client is. The client should usually be the entity, instructed by someone with authority recorded in its minute book. Advice instructed by the wrong person, for the wrong entity, is a gap both in privilege and in authority.

Recap

A company is a separate person acting through shareholders, directors and officers. It decides by resolution, records in its minute book, and signs within a written authority matrix. Watch apparent authority and pre-incorporation contracts. Canada and Guyana both expect companies to know who controls them. Next: Omar on The Numbers, a flow of funds through a two-tier structure.
checklist: Record which hat you wear for each decision: shareholder, director or officer
Pass and date the resolution before signing the document it approves
Keep the minute book complete, including registers and conflicts
Write a signing authority matrix with amounts and second signatories
Give counterparties a copy of the signing authority at contract signing
Form the company before signing, or sign for an entity to be formed with a release
Keep the record of individuals with significant control current
Fix a missing resolution by truthful ratification, never by backdating
head: Field checklist
speak: A company is a separate legal person, the principle taught through the Salomon case, but it has no hands. It acts through shareholders, who own it, directors, who manage it and owe it duties, and officers, who run its day-to-day affairs. It decides by resolution, at a meeting or in writing, and some decisions need a higher shareholder majority. The minute book holds the constating documents, registers, minutes and resolutions, and conflicts of interest. Lenders want a certified resolution dated before you sign, and proof of who holds office. Authority can be actual or apparent, so keep a written signing matrix and show it to counterparties. Contracts signed before the company exists can bind you personally. Canada and Guyana both increasingly expect companies to record who really owns and controls them. Never backdate a resolution; ratify truthfully.
terms: Resolution — a formal decision of a company's directors or shareholders, passed at a meeting or in writing.
Apparent authority — authority an outsider can reasonably believe a person has because of how the company presented them.
Ratification — a later formal approval that adopts an act done earlier without authority.

hostile.q: The loan resolution in your minute book is dated two days after you signed the commitment letter. Was the borrower ever authorised?
hostile.a: The commitment was signed before the formal resolution, which should not have happened. The directors have now passed a resolution ratifying the signature, dated truthfully, and my counsel will confirm its effect in the closing opinion. From now on, the resolution is passed and certified before any loan document is signed.

title: Following the money through a two-tier structure
summary: A worked flow of funds from a project company that has sold its building, through a holding company, to the owner: lender repaid, tax inside the project company, loans and capital returned, dividends paid, and the cost of taking money out personally. Every rate is hypothetical and labelled as such.
body:
Mr Shabazz, a structure chart only becomes real when you push a dollar through it and watch where it stops, what it pays and what reaches you. Today we follow one project's sale proceeds from the buyer's cheque to your personal account.

Recall

Q. Why does a construction lender usually want a special purpose vehicle as borrower?

A. Because a single-purpose entity owns only the project, so the lender's security and the borrower's obligations are not mixed with other projects' risks and creditors.

Q. In a joint venture waterfall, what must the distributions always sum to?

A. The cash available to the partners after the lender is repaid: their capital plus the profit. If the totals do not match, a tier is wrong.

Q. If the cap rate on a building rises from 5 to 6 percent with net operating income unchanged, what happens to its value?

A. It falls by about one sixth. At 600,000 dollars of net operating income, value drops from 12 million to 10 million dollars.

Why this matters

Owners often know their structure's shape and not its arithmetic. They cannot say how much of a profit stays in the project company, how much reaches the holding company, and how much reaches them, or what happens to their personal liquidity when the money is trapped one level up. Walking the numbers once, carefully, turns the chart into something you can explain to a lender, a partner and yourself.

The structure

Hypothetical. You own a holding company, Holdco. Holdco owns all the shares of a project company, the SPV, which built and sold a building. Holdco funded the SPV's equity of 7.5 million dollars in two forms: 500,000 dollars as share capital, and 7 million dollars as a documented shareholder loan, meaning money lent by the owner to its own company on written terms. Funding mostly by loan is a common choice because repaying a loan is usually not a taxable distribution, but its treatment, and any limits on it, depend on the system; verify against the primary source.

The rates below are invented for teaching and are not any jurisdiction's actual rates: tax on the SPV's profit at 25 percent, no tax on a dividend from the SPV to Holdco, and personal tax on a dividend from Holdco to you at 15 percent.

Worked example one: from sale to Holdco

  1. Sale. The SPV sells the building for 28 million dollars.
  2. Lender repaid. The construction loan and its interest, 15.5 million dollars, are repaid first, because the lender is secured on the building. Cash left in the SPV: 28 minus 15.5 equals 12.5 million.
  3. Profit. The 12.5 million is the 7.5 million of equity plus 5 million of taxable profit, after all costs, which we take as given.
  4. Tax inside the SPV. 25 percent of 5 million equals 1.25 million dollars. Cash left: 12.5 minus 1.25 equals 11.25 million.
  5. Shareholder loan repaid to Holdco. 7 million dollars. Cash left in the SPV: 4.25 million.
  6. Dividend of after-tax profit to Holdco. 5 million minus 1.25 million equals 3.75 million dollars. Cash left in the SPV: 500,000, which is its share capital.
  7. Share capital returned. On winding up the SPV, the 500,000 dollars returns to Holdco, after a formal resolution and any steps the statute requires.

Check: Holdco receives 7 million plus 3.75 million plus 500,000, which is 11.25 million dollars, matching the cash left after tax in step 4. The total leakage so far is the 1.25 million of SPV tax, 25 percent of the profit.

Say that out loud now.

Lender first, then tax, then loans, then dividends, then capital. And the totals must match.

Worked example two: from Holdco to you

Holdco now holds 11.25 million dollars. Two choices.

  • Keep it working. Holdco lends 9 million dollars into the next project's SPV. No second layer of tax arises yet, under these hypothetical rates. The second layer is deferred, not avoided.
  • Take the profit out. Holdco pays you the 3.75 million of profit as a dividend. Personal tax at 15 percent is 562,500 dollars. You receive 3,187,500 dollars.

Total leakage if all the profit comes out: 1.25 million plus 562,500 equals 1,812,500 dollars on 5 million of profit, an effective 36.25 percent under these invented rates. If Holdco keeps it working, leakage today is 25 percent. Whether deferral is worth it depends on what the next project earns and on rules about money left in holding companies, which some systems restrict; verify against the primary source and take licensed tax advice.

Worked example three: grossing up for your liquidity floor

Now the personal side. Suppose your living costs and liquidity floor need 300,000 dollars of personal cash this year, and everything else stays in Holdco. How large a dividend must Holdco pay?

  1. You keep 85 percent of each dividend dollar at the hypothetical 15 percent rate.
  2. Required dividend: 300,000 divided by 0.85 equals about 352,941 dollars.
  3. Tax: 352,941 minus 300,000 equals about 52,941 dollars.

Dividing the cash you need by the share you keep is called grossing up. It is the number you plan, not the net figure, and it must be approved by a Holdco directors' resolution declaring the dividend, recorded in the minute book. Day 4 explained why.

How the lender reads the same schedule

Your construction lender looks at the shareholder loan very differently from you. To you it is your capital, repayable without a distribution. To the lender it is a competing creditor inside its borrower. So lenders commonly require the shareholder loan to be subordinated and postponed, meaning it ranks behind the construction loan and cannot be repaid while the construction loan is outstanding. That is commercial practice, not a standard, and the exact terms are negotiated. It is why step 2 above repays the lender before step 5 repays Holdco, and why you should never plan to recover your shareholder loan early from an interim refinancing without the lender's written consent. If you model the flow of funds in the wrong order, you will show yourself cash that the loan agreement forbids you to take, and you will find out at the worst time.

Where structures leak by accident

Three common surprises. Paying a personal expense from the SPV, which can be treated as a taxable benefit or a distribution and muddies the books. Failing to document the shareholder loan, so its repayment is later treated as a dividend. And winding up an SPV before every liability is settled, so a later warranty claim finds no defendant except, possibly, you. Each is avoided by records, not cleverness. Professional sign-off required: a licensed tax adviser on the flow of funds and a corporate lawyer on the dividends, loan and winding up.

The biggest risk

Planning on rates you remember rather than rates you have verified. A single wrong rate can reverse the choice between retaining and extracting. The control is a flow-of-funds schedule, updated by your adviser each year, with the source of every rate written beside it.

The beginner's mistake

Treating money in Holdco as personal cash. It is not yours to spend until a dividend or loan repayment is properly approved and taxed, and it may be needed by the next project.

Callback

In Week 15, Elias and Sage taught after-tax leakage as the gap between pre-tax and after-tax returns. This lesson shows where in the structure that gap opens: inside the project company, and again on the way to you, with timing deciding how much opens today.

Recap

Push the sale proceeds through in order: lender, tax, shareholder loan, dividend, share capital, with totals that match. Decide whether profit stays working in Holdco or comes out, knowing that deferral is not avoidance. Gross up the dividend you need for your liquidity floor and approve it properly. Next: Omar in The Room, opening a bank account and closing a loan when the banker asks who controls the company.
checklist: Draw the structure chart with every entity and the form of each funding
Document every shareholder loan in writing
Push sale proceeds through in order: lender, tax, loans, dividends, capital
Check that what each level receives matches the cash available
Compare retaining and extracting profit on verified rates
Gross up the dividend needed for your personal liquidity floor
Approve every dividend by directors' resolution in the minute book
Settle all liabilities before winding up an SPV
head: Field checklist
speak: Follow the money through a two-tier structure. Holdco owns the project SPV and funded it with 500,000 dollars of share capital and a 7 million dollar documented shareholder loan. The SPV sells for 28 million, repays the lender 15.5 million and has 12.5 million left: the 7.5 million of equity plus 5 million of profit. With an invented 25 percent tax, 1.25 million goes in tax. The SPV repays the 7 million loan, pays a 3.75 million dividend, and returns its 500,000 of capital on winding up, so Holdco receives 11.25 million. If Holdco pays the profit out to you at an invented 15 percent, you receive about 3.19 million, and total leakage is 36.25 percent. If it keeps the money working, the second layer is deferred, not avoided. To net 300,000 dollars personally, gross it up: about 353,000 of dividend.
terms: Shareholder loan — money an owner lends to its own company on written terms, repayable as debt rather than distributed as profit.
Flow of funds — the ordered path money takes through a structure, showing what each entity receives and pays.
Gross-up — calculating the pre-tax amount needed to leave a target amount after tax.

hostile.q: You funded the SPV almost entirely with a shareholder loan. Aren't you just disguising profit as loan repayments to avoid tax?
hostile.a: No. The loan was documented when the money went in, its repayment returns exactly the 7 million that was advanced, and the profit is taxed in the SPV and paid as a dividend. The loan is the return of my own capital, not the profit. My tax adviser has reviewed the funding against the rules on debt and equity, and the advice is in the file.

title: Who controls this company? The banker's desk and the closing call
summary: Two meetings test whether your entity is real: opening its bank account, where the banker must know who owns and controls it, and the loan closing call, where the lender's counsel checks every resolution and signature. This lesson scripts both, with the lines to say, the lines never to say, the question behind the question, and when to stay silent.
body:
Mr Shabazz, a banker and a lender's lawyer ask the same question in different words: who really owns this company, who controls it, and can you prove it? Arrive with the answer on paper and these meetings are routine. Arrive without it and they become an interrogation.

Recall

Q. In the composite pre-formation case, what was the root cause?

A. No boundary between the developer's personal money and the project's money before the company existed, so nothing could prove which side a cost fell on.

Q. At a landowner's kitchen table, what do you never do at the first meeting?

A. Sign anything. You leave a plain-language summary, encourage independent advice, and sign later with both lawyers' comments in hand.

Q. How do you answer an investor who wants to buy at the top of a cycle because prices "only go up"?

A. With the reference class: show what happened to values and credit in past downturns, and test the deal at the downside case before committing.

Why this matters

Banks are required in most systems to identify their customers, understand who ultimately owns and controls them, and understand where their money comes from. This is often called know-your-customer, and it sits inside anti-money-laundering law. Lenders add their own layer at closing: they will not fund until their counsel is satisfied the borrower exists, is in good standing, decided to borrow and is signing through authorised people. Neither is personal. Both are where a poorly kept entity is exposed, and a delayed account or closing can cost a site or a rate lock.

Room one: opening the account

The scene. A bank branch, a relationship banker with a compliance checklist. You are opening an account for a new project SPV owned by your holding company. You bring a folder.

What is in the folder: the SPV's certificate and constating documents, the register of directors and shareholders, the Holdco's same documents, a one-page entity chart showing that you ultimately own and control both, a directors' resolution opening the account and naming signatories, identification for each signatory, and a short note on the source of the initial deposit, for example "equity from Holdco, funded from the sale proceeds of a completed project," with the closing statement attached.

Lines to say:

  • "Here is the structure on one page. I am the individual who ultimately owns and controls both companies."
  • "The first deposit comes from Holdco. Here is the document showing where Holdco's funds came from."
  • "The resolution names two signatories, with two signatures required above 50,000 dollars."
  • "If anything else is needed for your review, tell me and I will send it by Friday."

Lines never to say:

  • "It is just my company, so just put me on the account." The bank needs the company's authority, not your assurance.
  • "The money came from various places." It sounds like concealment even when it is not.
  • "Can we skip the ownership form? It is a formality." It is a legal requirement for the bank.

The question behind the question. When the banker asks, "Who else has an interest in these companies?", the real question is, "Is someone hidden behind you?" If you have a partner, a trust or a nominee anywhere, say so plainly and show it on the chart. An undisclosed interest discovered later can close the account and damage the relationship for good.

Worked example one: the source-of-funds note

Hypothetical. You will deposit 1.5 million dollars of equity. The note reads: "Funds are transferred from Holdco's account, where they were received on the sale of a completed building owned by its subsidiary. Attached: the sale closing statement, the lender's discharge, and Holdco's bank statement showing receipt." Three attachments turn a question into a file. Without them, the deposit may be held while the bank investigates, which can take days you do not have before a land closing.

Say that out loud now.

"Here is who owns it, who controls it, where the money came from, and who can sign."

Keeping the folder alive

The folder is not a one-time exercise. Every bank you use, every lender and many buyers will ask for the same documents, and they will want them current. Keep a master version for each entity, updated whenever a director, officer, signatory or owner changes, with the date of the last update on its cover page. A change you forget to tell the bank about, such as a new partner or a departed signatory, is exactly what a compliance review is designed to find, and finding it yourself first is far better than having it found.

Room two: the closing call

The scene. A video call two days before a construction loan funds. The lender's counsel, your lawyer, you. Counsel works through a closing agenda.

Counsel asks for: a certificate of status showing the SPV is in good standing; a certified copy of its constating documents; a certified directors' resolution approving the loan and the security and authorising named officers to sign; an incumbency certificate confirming who holds those offices, with specimen signatures; the same items for Holdco if it gives a guarantee; and your lawyer's opinion that the borrower is validly existing and has authorised the documents.

Lines to say:

  • "My counsel will circulate the certified resolution and the incumbency certificate today."
  • "The resolution was passed on the 3rd; the commitment letter was signed on the 5th."
  • "I will confirm that with my lawyer and come back to you within the hour."

Lines never to say:

  • "We can paper the resolution after funding." That invites a misstatement to a lender.
  • "I am the director, so my signature is enough for everything." The documents may require a second signatory, and the guarantee is signed in a different capacity.

Worked example two: when the dates do not line up

Counsel notices that the SPV signed the commitment letter on the 5th, but the minute book shows no resolution until the 9th. Do not argue and do not explain at length. Say: "That is correct. The commitment was signed before the resolution. We will pass a ratifying resolution today, dated today, and my counsel will address it in the opinion." Then stop. Counsel's job is to find gaps; your job is to close them truthfully. A truthful fix is routine. An invented date is not.

When to stay silent, and how to hold your state

When counsel reads through a checklist, let them finish before answering any item. Interrupting to defend one point often draws attention to the next. Keep your own one-page closing checklist beside you and tick items as they are confirmed. If you feel your pulse rise at a question you cannot answer, slow down and say, "I will confirm that and reply today." Composure on these calls is mostly preparation: the folder does the talking.

The biggest risk

Hiding or blurring an owner to make the meeting faster. In anti-money-laundering systems, concealment is the thing banks are trained to look for. The control: an accurate entity chart, including every partner, trust and nominee, given to the bank and the lender at the start.

The beginner's mistake

Leaving the closing deliverables to the lawyers alone. Your lawyer can draft the resolution, but only you know whether the decision was really made and when. Review the closing agenda yourself a week ahead.

Callback

In Week 24, Elias and Cole taught the difference between arrangements that are lawful and those that hide facts. Know-your-customer and the closing call are where that line is tested in practice: everything you show the bank should be complete and true, because the obligation to know who owns and controls the company now falls on both of you.

Recap

At the bank, bring the folder: constating documents, registers, an entity chart, the account resolution, identification and a documented source of funds. On the closing call, deliver certified resolutions dated before signing, incumbency and good standing, and fix any gap truthfully. Next: Kema closes the week with six questions, a Red Pen resolution and the boardroom drill.
checklist: Prepare an entity chart naming every owner, partner, trust and nominee
Bring constating documents and registers for every entity in the chain
Pass a resolution opening each account and naming signatories with limits
Document the source of every initial deposit with attachments
Review the lender's closing agenda yourself a week before closing
Deliver certified resolutions dated before the documents they approve
Fix any date gap by a truthful ratifying resolution
Answer what you do not know with a specific time to confirm
head: Field checklist
speak: A banker and a lender's lawyer both want to know who really owns the company, who controls it, and whether you can prove it. At the bank, bring a folder: the SPV's and Holdco's constating documents and registers, a one-page entity chart, a resolution opening the account and naming signatories with limits, identification, and a source-of-funds note with the closing statement attached. If there is a partner, trust or nominee anywhere, show it; an undisclosed interest found later can close the account. On the closing call, counsel will ask for good standing, a certified resolution, an incumbency certificate and your lawyer's opinion. If the dates do not line up, say so, pass a truthful ratifying resolution, and stop talking. Never offer to paper the resolution after funding. The folder does the talking.
terms: Know-your-customer — the process by which a bank identifies its customer, its ultimate owners and controllers, and the source of its funds.
Incumbency certificate — a certificate confirming who holds an entity's offices, often with their specimen signatures.
Certificate of status — an official record that an entity exists and is in good standing with its registry.

hostile.q: Your chart shows a trust holding 20 percent of Holdco. Who are its beneficiaries, and why wasn't that on the first form?
hostile.a: The trust is a hypothetical family trust holding a minority interest; here is the trust deed extract naming the trustee and beneficiaries, as your form requires. It should have been on the first form and I apologise for the omission. Nothing else in the chain is held for anyone not shown. I will sign the updated declaration today.

role: Chief of staff and learning coach
title: Entities week review: six questions, a Red Pen resolution and the boardroom
summary: Six questions on choosing the vehicle, pre-formation spending, running costs and leakage, resolutions and authority, and the flow of funds, then a recap of the week. The Red Pen drill plants defects in a hypothetical directors' resolution, and the boardroom drill asks you to explain your structure in two minutes.
body:
Mr Shabazz, this week's lesson is that an entity protects you only if it is chosen for a reason and run as a real, separate person. Today you test whether you can explain both, and spot the gaps in a document that claims to prove them.

Recall

Q. What does an extra special purpose vehicle cost, and what does it buy?

A. A yearly running cost for filings, books, accounts and bank fees, in this week's example about 8,000 dollars each. It buys a ring-fence that keeps one project's losses from reaching another project's equity.

Q. What were the nine defects in last fortnight's Red Pen option letter, in short?

A. An agreement to agree on the uplift, a vague term, a refundable premium, no exercise mechanics, open-ended extensions, no attached purchase agreement, no assignment right, a signatory without proven authority, and no governing law, registration or independent advice.

Q. What does timing in a property cycle do to a developer's choice of when to sell?

A. It changes the exit cap rate and the depth of the buyer pool. Selling into tightening credit usually means a higher cap rate and a lower price, so the exit plan must be tested at the downside.

Why this matters

Structure is often treated as paperwork that lawyers handle. In practice you will be asked about it by every lender, partner, banker and buyer you deal with, and you will sign documents in its name every month. If you can explain why each entity exists and show that it is run properly, you look like an owner who can be trusted with money. Answer each question aloud before reading the answer.

The six questions

Question 1. Name the five questions that choose a vehicle.

Answer: Liability, tax, financing, governance, and exit and estate, answered for these particular owners.

Question 2. Why can ring-fencing through special purpose vehicles fail?

Answer: Because a personal guarantee or a guarantee from another entity reaches across it, and because a court may disregard an entity that was misused or not run as a separate person.

Question 3. In the composite pre-formation case, why did the developer receive credit for only 175,000 of the 250,000 dollars he spent?

Answer: Because only 140,000 was clearly provable, half of 70,000 invoiced to another company was accepted, and 40,000 of undocumented spending was not credited.

Question 4. What is the difference between actual and apparent authority?

Answer: Actual authority is what the company actually granted. Apparent authority is what an outsider can reasonably believe a person has from how the company presented them, which can sometimes bind the company anyway.

Question 5. In Day 5's flow of funds, what was the effective leakage if all the profit was paid out to the owner, and why did it fall if Holdco kept the money working?

Answer: 36.25 percent under the invented rates. Keeping it in Holdco deferred the personal layer of tax, leaving only the 25 percent paid in the project company for now. Deferred is not avoided.

Question 6. What was Rule 35?

Answer: From the first dollar, every project cost is logged, paid from one source, invoiced to the project or an entity to be formed, and assignable to it; nothing is moved into the company later on my word alone.

Say that out loud now.

Say Rule 35 without looking, then name the three documents that make an entity real.

Recap of the week

Day 1, Omar: the vehicle types, the five questions, one SPV per project, and the minute book, resolutions and signing authority. Day 2, Ford with Cole: a composite developer whose pre-formation spending could not be proved. Day 3, Nadia: running costs against ring-fenced exposure, leakage on three paths, visible equity, and Warrick on after-extraction value. Day 4, LEX: the separate person, the three groups, resolutions, minute books, actual and apparent authority, pre-incorporation contracts, and a Canada and Guyana comparison. Day 5, Omar: a flow of funds from sale to Holdco to you, with a gross-up for your liquidity floor. Day 6, Omar: the banker's know-your-customer folder and the lender's closing call.

Red Pen drill

Read this hypothetical directors' resolution and find the defects before reading on.

Resolution of the directors of Project Co, hypothetical. Dated: to be confirmed. Resolved that the company borrow from the bank on the terms discussed, and that Mr Shabazz or anyone he nominates may sign all documents. Resolved that the company grant a guarantee for the obligations of its affiliate. Resolved that the company pay the costs Mr Shabazz incurred before incorporation, as he will advise. Signed: Mr Shabazz, director. Note: the second director will sign when available; Mr Shabazz is also the borrower's general contractor's part owner.

The defects, revealed:

  1. "Dated: to be confirmed." A resolution must carry its true date, before the documents it approves are signed.
  2. "On the terms discussed." Identify the lender, the amount and the commitment letter by date, and approve the documents and the security.
  3. "Anyone he nominates." An open-ended delegation defeats the signing matrix. Name the officers, their capacities and any second-signature requirement.
  4. A guarantee of an affiliate's obligations. A guarantee can weaken the ring-fence and may need specific approval, a benefit to the company and, in some systems, shareholder approval. Verify against the primary source.
  5. Pre-incorporation costs "as he will advise." Rule 35 broken. Attach an agreed schedule of costs with evidence.
  6. One director signing for a board of two. A written resolution generally needs every director entitled to vote, and a meeting needs a quorum. Check the articles.
  7. An undisclosed conflict of interest. His interest in the general contractor must be disclosed and recorded, and he may need to abstain from related decisions.

Boardroom drill

Set a two-minute timer and explain your structure to an imaginary investment committee. Then compare with the model.

Model answer: "Each project sits in its own special purpose vehicle, owned by a holding company I control. We chose that by five questions: liability, tax, financing, governance and exit. The SPV ring-fences each project's losses, though guarantees can cross that fence, so we sign them only by specific resolution. Each entity is run as a separate person: a current minute book, resolutions passed and dated before the documents they approve, a written signing matrix with second signatures above set limits, and conflicts disclosed. Every project cost is logged from the first dollar and paid from the SPV's own account, so our equity is provable to lenders. Profit flows lender first, then tax, then loan and dividend to Holdco, and only what I need personally comes out. Our lawyer, accountant and tax adviser review the structure together each year."

Score yourself

Score your attempt from 1 to 5 on accuracy, structure, composure and the hard question. Accuracy: were the terms and the order of the flow of funds correct? Structure: bottom line first, then reasons, then controls? Composure: did you pause rather than rush? The hard question: did you say what happens when a guarantee crosses the ring-fence? Reread only the lesson behind your lowest score.

The biggest risk

Designing a careful structure and then running it carelessly. The control is a corporate calendar for every entity, with filings, annual resolutions and minute book reviews, owned by one named person.

The beginner's mistake

Studying by rereading. Close the lesson and answer aloud; the effort of recall is what makes it stay.

Callback

In Week 8, Tessa and Warrick taught the will and powers of attorney. Your shares in Holdco and its SPVs are assets that pass under your estate plan, and a power of attorney decides who could vote them if you could not. A structure without an estate plan stops working at exactly the moment it is needed.

Recap

head: The six questions
speak: An entity protects you only if it is chosen for a reason and run as a real, separate person. Choose the vehicle by five questions: liability, tax, financing, governance, and exit and estate. Put each project in its own special purpose vehicle under a holding company, remembering that guarantees cross the ring-fence. Run each entity through a current minute book, resolutions passed and dated before the documents they approve, and a written signing matrix. Disclose conflicts. Log every cost from the first dollar and pay it from the SPV's own account, because unprovable spending is lost. Price the running cost of each entity against the exposure it protects, and model leakage on verified rates. Money flows lender first, then tax, then loans and dividends to Holdco, and deferral is not avoidance. Rule 35 keeps the first dollar clean.
terms: Quorum — the minimum number of directors or shareholders who must be present for a meeting's decisions to be valid.
Conflict of interest disclosure — a director's formal statement of a personal interest in a company contract, recorded in the minutes.
Corporate calendar — a schedule of every entity's filings, annual resolutions and record reviews, with a named owner.

hostile.q: Your SPV guarantees its affiliate's loan. Then what exactly is your ring-fence protecting?
hostile.a: Less than it would without the guarantee, and I would rather say so than hide it. The guarantee was approved by a specific resolution, is capped and is disclosed on the entity chart. Every other liability of the affiliate stays inside the affiliate. If the guarantee were unlimited, the ring-fence would be largely gone, which is why we negotiated the cap before signing.
